rows: Model training and artifact persistence flow

text: This report documents a wind energy forecasting workspace that has been reorganized into separate frontend and backend roots and then extended into a date-based seven-day forecast experience. The frontend is implemented in Next.js and React, while the backend is implemented in FastAPI and serves both model metadata and forecast endpoints. The core prediction layer uses a saved machine learning model to estimate future wind power output from weather conditions.

The system begins with a city search and date selection in the browser. The backend then queries the Open-Meteo geocoding and forecast APIs to fetch the hourly weather variables required by the model. A recursive prediction loop appends each future hourly weather row to a seeded recent-history window, predicts wind power for that hour, and feeds that prediction back into the history so later hours can use lagged and rolling features that remain consistent with the trained model interface.

The workspace currently uses a synthetic dataset of 5000 hourly rows ranging from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 to 2025-07-28 07:00:00. The saved best model is random_forest, operating with a lookback window of 24 rows and a minimum history requirement of 30 rows. The current results show a validation RMSE of 29.814 and a test RMSE of 29.310, which positions the application as a prototype forecasting platform suitable for workflow demonstration and further refinement.
Keywords: Wind energy forecasting, Next.js, FastAPI, Open-Meteo, recursive prediction, random forest, hourly weather data.

Wind energy forecasting is a time-sensitive problem because operational planning depends on knowing how much energy may be produced in the near future. In practical applications, the forecast is useful for scheduling, balancing, monitoring, and communicating likely production to users or operators.

A modern forecasting interface should not force users to upload raw history files or manually craft JSON payloads. Instead, a user should be able to choose a location and a date, allow the system to fetch weather data automatically, and receive a meaningful daily and hourly forecast view.

The original workspace centered on model training and raw prediction requests, but it did not expose a convenient end-user forecasting flow. The challenge addressed in this project is to transform the repository into a user-facing system that predicts wind energy for a selected date and the following six days by using live weather inputs from Open-Meteo.
The first objective is to segregate the project into a clean frontend and backend structure at the repository root.
The second objective is to replace the manual prediction interface with a date-based seven-day forecasting experience.
The third objective is to preserve the saved model artifacts and reuse them in a recursive hourly forecast loop.
The fourth objective is to explain the full user flow, architecture, and limitations in a formal project report.

The implemented scope includes repository restructuring, backend API design, Open-Meteo integration, recursive forecasting logic, a Next.js user interface, and project-level documentation. Model retraining was kept optional, and the current saved artifacts remain part of the delivered system.

The main gap in the earlier workflow was the absence of an experience aligned with how a real user thinks about forecasting: place plus date, not feature arrays plus timestamps. The proposed direction maps that user intent to a layered implementation consisting of weather retrieval, feature-compatible history seeding, recursive prediction, daily aggregation, and clear frontend presentation.

The frontend stack is Next.js ^15.0.0, React ^19.0.0, and TypeScript ^5.6.0. The backend stack is FastAPI, Uvicorn, pandas, scikit-learn, and joblib. TensorFlow support remains optional for the neural network paths.

Model training, evaluation, and preprocessing live in Python modules under backend/src, while the user experience and API client live in the Next.js application under frontend/app, frontend/components, and frontend/lib.

The repository now uses two clearly separated root-level folders. The frontend folder contains the Next.js application, UI components, configuration, and package management files. The backend folder contains the FastAPI service, source modules, model artifacts, plots, notebooks, dataset files, and Python dependencies.

This segregation improves readability, makes startup commands clearer, and aligns the implementation with typical full stack deployment thinking where the user interface and server runtime evolve independently.

The backend/app directory contains the FastAPI entry point and request models. The backend/src directory contains preprocessing, prediction, training, evaluation, data generation, weather helpers, and recursive forecasting logic.

The backend/models directory stores model_metadata.json, model_comparison.csv, preprocessor.joblib, and the saved random_forest artifact. The backend/data directory stores the synthetic wind_data.csv dataset used for training and for forecast seeding.

The frontend/app directory holds the App Router entry files such as layout.tsx and page.tsx. The frontend/components directory holds the main ForecastStudio component that powers the forecast experience. The frontend/lib directory contains the typed API client used by the UI to call the FastAPI backend.
This structure keeps each concern local and makes it straightforward to identify where to change layout, styling, network contracts, or business logic.

The project ships with a synthetic dataset containing 5000 hourly rows. The timestamp span runs from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 to 2025-07-28 07:00:00, giving the model a continuous sequence of weather and power observations for experimentation and demonstration.

The principal raw columns are timestamp, wind_speed, wind_direction, temperature, pressure, and power_output. Additional convenience columns such as hour, day, and month are also stored in the CSV output created by the synthetic data generator.

The dataset is created by backend/src/generate_synthetic_data.py. The generator simulates hourly weather signals, including seasonality and daily cycles for temperature, pressure, and wind speed, then derives wind direction through a persistent drifting process.

Power output is synthesized by combining a cubic power-curve relationship with wind speed, a wake-loss adjustment based on direction, an air-density adjustment influenced by pressure and temperature, and random noise. This design produces a realistic-enough shape for model pipeline testing, even though it is not a real wind farm measurement stream.

The preprocessing layer validates required columns, parses timestamps, sorts data chronologically, fills numeric missing values with medians, and removes outliers for selected variables using an interquartile range based rule. This reduces obviously distorted points before training begins.

Feature engineering adds hour, day, month, and dayofweek fields from the timestamp. Wind direction is transformed into sine and cosine form so the cyclical nature of angular data can be modeled more smoothly than with raw degree values alone.

Lagged features are created for wind speed, temperature, pressure, and power output at one, two, and three previous steps. Rolling mean features are then calculated for wind speed and power output using windows of three and six observations.
The saved model metadata lists 25 engineered feature columns. The preprocessor reserves 6 warm-up rows for lag and rolling statistics and requires a minimum of 30 recent rows to run inference safely.

For sequence-oriented models such as the optional LSTM, the preprocessor also creates rolling input sequences using the configured lookback window. The current lookback size is 24 rows, which allows the system to represent temporal behavior beyond a single tabular snapshot.

The training workflow is implemented in backend/src/train.py. It prepares the dataset, fits the available models, measures validation and test metrics, saves trained artifacts, and writes model metadata that the inference layer later uses.

The training pipeline seeds its random number generators for reproducibility and then evaluates models using MAE, RMSE, and R2. Artifacts are written into backend/models so the application can run even without retraining every time.

The workspace defines three model builders in backend/src/models.py: a RandomForestRegressor baseline, a dense feed-forward neural network, and an LSTM network. The tree-based model works in standard tabular mode, while the LSTM works on generated sequences.

In the current environment, TensorFlow is optional and may not be available or practical on Python 3.13. As a result, the workspace presently relies on the saved random forest model as the active forecasting artifact.

The current saved best model is random_forest. The random forest configuration uses 300 trees with a maximum depth of 14, a minimum samples split of 4, and a minimum samples leaf value of 2. This model is light enough to serve predictions quickly through the FastAPI backend.
The saved comparison row reports validation MAE = 24.805, validation RMSE = 29.814, validation R2 = -0.017, test MAE = 24.273, test RMSE = 29.310, and test R2 = -0.008.

The negative R2 values show that the current model should be treated as a prototype estimate rather than a production-calibrated energy predictor. This is consistent with the synthetic nature of the dataset and the demonstration-focused scope of the workspace.

The backend keeps model_metadata.json, model_comparison.csv, preprocessor.joblib, and random_forest.joblib together so the inference path can load them consistently. Compatibility aliases were also added to preserve loading behavior after the repository reorganization.

The FastAPI application is defined in backend/app/main.py. It configures the API metadata, registers CORS middleware for local Next.js origins, and exposes the routes used by the frontend and any raw integration tests.

The root endpoint returns API metadata and route pointers for the user interface. The /health endpoint provides a simple online status check. The /model-info endpoint returns saved artifact metadata, comparison availability, and recent-history requirements.

The /demo-window endpoint exposes a recent slice of the synthetic dataset for compatibility and inspection. The /locations/search endpoint queries Open-Meteo geocoding for city lookup. The /forecast endpoint is the main user-facing route used by the new Next.js experience, while /predict remains available as a direct recent-history prediction API for compatibility.

The backend uses Pydantic models to validate location details and the requested forecast date. Forecast validation errors map to HTTP 400, configuration issues map to HTTP 503, Open-Meteo failures map to HTTP 502, and unexpected conditions map to HTTP 500.

This route-level separation is important because the frontend presents different user messages depending on whether the problem is a bad request, a missing local artifact, or an upstream weather-provider issue.

The older /predict route was deliberately retained even after the UI redesign. This keeps the backend useful for raw JSON or programmatic prediction calls while the frontend moves to the richer forecast flow.

Location search is handled by backend/src/open_meteo.py. The search_locations helper queries the Open-Meteo geocoding endpoint and returns normalized records containing name, country, admin1, latitude, longitude, and timezone. The frontend consumes these typed results directly.

The fetch_hourly_forecast helper requests hourly variables aligned with the model feature requirements: temperature_2m, surface_pressure, wind_speed_10m, and wind_direction_10m. The request uses timezone=auto and wind_speed_unit=ms so the returned values are suitable for local-date aggregation and model input compatibility.
The backend also validates the returned payload rigorously. Missing arrays, unequal array lengths, missing values, and malformed JSON are all surfaced as weather provider errors.

The forecast engine enforces a fixed seven-day window. Because Open-Meteo supports a maximum forward horizon of sixteen days for this use case, the selected start date must leave room for the full seven-day block. The frontend therefore constrains the date picker, and the backend validates the same rule again.

A critical design decision in the forecasting engine is the use of seed history from backend/data/wind_data.csv. The engine loads the latest minimum required rows from the dataset, verifies that all inference columns are present, sorts timestamps, and converts them into the recent-history payload expected by the preprocessor.
This seed history provides the 30-row context needed for lagged and rolling features. Without it, the model could not build a valid input row for the first predicted hour.

For each future hourly weather record returned by Open-Meteo, the backend appends a new row to the history, temporarily filling power_output with the last known or last predicted value. The prediction helper then computes the next output using the already-loaded model runtime.

After prediction, the engine writes the predicted value back into the just-appended row so that later lag and rolling features can depend on recursively produced outputs. This chaining behavior is what makes the seven-day forecast possible even though the original model predicts one step at a time.

Once hourly predictions are produced, the backend aggregates them by local date. For each day, it computes total_energy as the sum of predicted hourly power values, average_power as the mean hourly prediction, peak_power as the maximum prediction, and peak_time as the timestamp where that maximum occurs.

The daily grouping is based on local timestamps returned by the weather provider and not on a hardcoded assumption of twenty-four rows per day. This protects the aggregation against timezone and daylight-saving transitions.

The frontend entry point is frontend/app/page.tsx, which renders the ForecastStudio component. Global metadata and styling are defined in layout.tsx and globals.css, keeping the user experience centered around a single dedicated forecast workspace.

The visible UI is now based on a location search box and a date picker instead of raw JSON or CSV inputs. As the user types a location, the frontend debounces the query, calls the backend /locations/search route, and presents matching cities in a selectable list.
Once a location is selected, the date picker enforces the supported forecast window. A single Forecast Wind Energy button triggers the backend /forecast request.
The UI highlights the selected day first. A summary band displays estimated daily energy, average power, peak hour output, and the model name used to generate the forecast.

Below that, a seven-day outlook section renders one card per day. The selected day is visually emphasized so the user immediately sees the day they asked about while still retaining the broader weekly context.

For the selected date, the interface shows an hourly table containing time, wind speed, direction, temperature, pressure, and predicted power. This provides a transparent bridge between weather conditions and forecast output.

The UI also reports backend status, the active model, seed history requirements, and human-readable feedback messages for loading, success, location-search errors, and forecast failures. This makes the application easier to understand and debug from the user side.
Step 1: The user opens the Next.js application in the browser.
Step 2: The frontend checks backend health and loads model information.
Step 3: The user searches for a city and chooses a forecast start date.
Step 4: The frontend posts the selected location and date to /forecast.
Step 5: The backend fetches hourly weather data from Open-Meteo for the selected seven-day window.
Step 6: The recursive forecast engine seeds itself with recent local history from backend/data/wind_data.csv.
Step 7: The backend predicts each future hour sequentially and aggregates daily totals.
Step 8: The frontend renders the selected day summary, the seven-day outlook, and the hourly breakdown table.

The workspace verification included FastAPI smoke checks, mocked forecast tests, and a frontend TypeScript typecheck. This confirms that the current contract between frontend and backend is internally consistent even though the final forecast accuracy remains dependent on the prototype dataset and saved artifact quality.

The project successfully shifted from a raw prediction workflow to a complete forecast application with a clear user flow. The frontend and backend are now separate at the root, the API exposes a forecast-oriented contract, and the user can request a date-based seven-day forecast without preparing manual history files.

The current saved metrics indicate prototype behavior: validation RMSE = 29.814, test RMSE = 29.310, and negative R2 scores on both splits. These results are acceptable for demonstrating the engineering workflow, but they also show that model quality still needs improvement before any operational use.
The project has a clean architectural separation between UI, API, and ML logic.
The forecast engine uses real weather inputs, which makes the interface more realistic than a static demo.
The recursive design respects the feature expectations of the trained model instead of bypassing them.
The frontend communicates status and uncertainty clearly by labeling results as estimates.

A notable design strength is that the current implementation reuses the saved model rather than discarding previous work. This reduces re-training friction and keeps the reporting faithful to the actual workspace state.

At the same time, the system inherits the limitations of its training source. Because the dataset is synthetic and site-agnostic, the forecast output should be understood as a workflow demonstration of wind-energy estimation, not a guarantee of real-world plant generation.
The current dataset is synthetic rather than sourced from a real wind farm or turbine telemetry stream.
The saved best model is a random forest that performs as a prototype baseline rather than a production predictor.
TensorFlow-backed models are optional and may not be convenient to train under Python 3.13 in the current environment.
The forecast engine depends on upstream weather availability from Open-Meteo.
Replace the synthetic dataset with real multi-site wind generation and meteorological history.
Introduce location-aware training so forecasts are calibrated to a specific geography or wind farm.
Store forecast histories and user queries for auditability and future evaluation.
Add comparative model selection, probabilistic bands, and uncertainty intervals.
Extend the frontend with charts, download options, and forecast history views.
Automate regression tests for both backend forecast contracts and frontend interactions.

The workspace has been transformed into a clearer and more practical wind energy forecasting application. The repository now separates frontend and backend responsibilities, and the user experience has moved from manual model input to a city-and-date driven forecast flow.

The backend combines saved model artifacts, weather retrieval, recent-history seeding, recursive prediction, and daily aggregation into a single API contract that the Next.js frontend can use directly. This produces a coherent demonstration of how an ML model can be embedded inside a full stack forecasting product.

Although the current model quality reflects the limitations of synthetic training data, the engineering structure is now strong enough to support better datasets, stronger models, richer visualization, and future deployment work.
